wine.name: Felton Road Block 5 Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from one block of The Elms Vineyard.
wine.sites: Block 5 of The Elms Vineyard at Bannockburn, planted in 1993 on a gentle north facing slope at the heart of the vineyard whose soils run from heavy loess and silt to clay and angular schist gravel, with old lake bed sediments reaching into its centre.
wine.making: Destemmed by gravity into the fermenters, with about a fifth kept as whole bunches in a vintage such as 2017, the fruit soaks for more than a week before a wild fermentation with indigenous yeasts, some three weeks on skins in all. It then spends sixteen to seventeen months in French oak barrels, a quarter to about a third of them new, and goes to bottle unfined and unfiltered.
wine.glass: Dark cherry, raspberry and crushed berries over rose petal, rhubarb, black tea and white pepper; darker and spicier than the house's other Pinot Noirs, with a stony edge, muscular yet fine tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Tight and muscular when young, it needs four or five years to open and then drinks well for a decade or more.
wine.serve: Pour at 15 to 17 degrees Celsius into a wide Burgundy glass; an hour or so in a decanter suits a young bottle.

records.table: Planted in 1993 and farmed biodynamically, one north facing block of The Elms Vineyard at Bannockburn gives Felton Road Block 5 Pinot Noir. Darker and spicier than the house's other Pinots and tight when young, it wants four or five years and then a decanter.
records.story: In 1990, by New Zealand Winegrowers' account, Felton Road's founder enrolled in the viticulture course at Lincoln University, and in 1991, the year the house dates its beginning to, he chose and laid out a vineyard just off Felton Road at Bannockburn, a district of old gold workings above the Kawarau. The first vines went in in 1992, and Block 5 followed in 1993 in what became The Elms Vineyard. In 1997 a young winemaker who had studied beside the founder at Lincoln made the first official Felton Road Pinot Noir, and in 2000 the founder sold the estate to a British wine lover. The house came to bottle the blocks of The Elms apart, Block 3 and Block 5 above all, and to farm its vineyards biodynamically, certified by Demeter and by BioGro, with wild yeasts in the cellar and no fining or filtering before bottling. Block 5's soils run from loess and silt to clay and schist gravel, with old lake bed sediments at its heart, and its wine is the darker and spicier of the two. The pair is a lesson in how far soil alone can move Pinot Noir within one vineyard.

report: Founded 1991 agrees with the library; the house's own sheets date site selection and vineyard design to 1991, Block 2 to 1992 and Block 5 to 1993, and New Zealand Winegrowers has the founder enrol at Lincoln in 1990, plant The Elms and see the first official Pinot Noir made in 1997, which the library's region record also gives.

Living people kept out: the founder (spelled Stewart and Stuart in the sources, not yet in people.json), the winemaker of 1997 and the buyer of 2000 (both already in people.json); the sale of 2000 rests on New Zealand Winegrowers and the Otago Daily Times, the buyer called British by the newspaper.

The making gathers the house's sheets by vintage: about a fifth whole bunch, a pre-fermentation soak of eight to ten days and twenty one to twenty three days on skins in 2017, sixteen months with thirty per cent new oak in 2017 and twenty five per cent in 2021, sixteen to seventeen months by the Block 3 and Block 5 sheet; hand picking was not confirmed and is not said.

The glass and ageing draw on the house's own notes (darker fruited and spicier than its other Pinots, a mineral note) and the critics its product pages quote (raspberry, rhubarb, rose petal, dark cherry; crushed berry, tea, white pepper; muscular tannin; four or five years to open, windows of about five to fifteen years from the vintage).
One merchant listing dates Block 5's first release to the 1999 vintage; with no second source the record gives no first year for the block's own bottling.

The library's region line and record call Felton Road the region's benchmark and its reference producer; the record does not, since the tab refuses a judgement, and the library's semi-continental in the traps sits beside the region record's continental, a small tension left for the integrator.

wine.name: Rippon Mature Vine Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Only Pinot Noir, from every fully grown vine of it on the estate.
wine.sites: The north facing escarpment on the western edge of Roy's Bay, Lake Wanaka, where glacial terminal moraines meet an ancient cone of coarse schist gravels; by the house's account its blocks include some of the oldest commercial vines in Central Otago.
wine.making: The fruit is picked by hand and fermented with wild yeasts; the wine then spends two winters in barrel, about eighteen months, with only a small share of new oak, and two years in bottle before it is released. It goes to bottle without fining or filtering.
wine.glass: Wild strawberry, dark cherry and plum over blueberry, mountain herbs and a note of mushroomy undergrowth, with crushed rock beneath; juicy and elegant rather than heavy, with fine, chalky tannin and a long, perfumed finish.
wine.ageing: It leaves the estate with years in bottle already, open and perfumed, and a strong vintage keeps and deepens for ten years and longer.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens in a carafe; a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: Above Lake Wanaka, where the family planted trial vines in 1975, every fully grown vine on schist and glacial gravel gives its fruit to Rippon Mature Vine Pinot Noir. It rests two winters in barrel and two years in bottle before release, and pours fine and perfumed.
records.story: The land at Roy's Bay on Lake Wanaka, part of the Wanaka Station the founder's grandfather had bought, has been farmed by his family since 1912, by the estate's own account. The founder had thought of growing grapes there since the Second World War, in which he served in submarines, and in 1973 he and his wife moved back to the family farm. In 1975 he planted a trial of some thirty grape varieties beside the lake, among the first vines of modern Central Otago, and in 1982, against the doubts of research bodies and local experts, he planted the first commercial block, the year from which the house dates its winegrowing. He became the founding president of the region's winegrowers' association. After his death his widow carried on the business they had founded, and their son went on to lead the vineyard and the cellar. The estate is farmed biodynamically. Mature Vine gathers all of its fully grown Pinot Noir and Jeunesse the younger vines, while two single blocks, Tinker's Field and Emma's Block, are bottled apart. The modern region's story goes back through this Pinot Noir to its trials of the 1970s, on a lakeside farm where the vines began as an experiment.

wine.name: Gibbston Valley Reserve Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir, grown in the house's own vineyards.
wine.sites: A few low yielding rows chosen in a strong vintage from the house's vineyards: the Home Block at Gibbston in the Kawarau Gorge, planted in 1983, and its sites at Bendigo, among them China Terrace and the higher School House.
wine.making: As the house tells it, a Reserve takes only a few rows of fruit in a great vintage and is made in small quantities, apart from its other Pinot Noirs. The house ages its Pinot Noir in barrel in the cave blasted into the schist behind the winery in 1995.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black cherry and dark plum with violets and anise, and cedar and toast from the barrel; deep, layered and long, the fruit dark rather than red.
wine.ageing: Generous from the start, it gains depth over several years in bottle in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius in a wide Burgundy glass; decanting a young bottle for an hour is optional.

records.table: Gibbston Valley released Central Otago's first commercial vintage in 1987, and its Reserve Pinot Noir is the house's pick of a few rows in a strong year. Its 2000 vintage took the Pinot Noir trophy at the International Wine Challenge in London in 2001.
records.story: Gibbston lies in the Kawarau Gorge between Queenstown and Cromwell, the highest of Central Otago's sub-regions, where the vines ripen later than in neighbouring districts. The house's founder planted his first vines there in the early 1980s, and in 1983, by the house's account, he planted its first commercial vineyard, the Home Block. In 1987 Gibbston Valley released the region's first commercial vintage, a date New Zealand Winegrowers gives for Gibbston's first commercial bottling. In 1990, in the house's own history, the founder established Gibbston Valley Wines as a boutique winery with a tasting room and a restaurant, and by 1995 the barrels had outgrown their store; rather than build another, he had a cave blasted into the schist mountainside behind the winery, New Zealand's largest wine cave by the house's own account. The house came to grow at Bendigo too, on the warmer terraces by Lake Dunstan, where China Terrace and School House give its single vineyard wines. The Reserve is its selection of a few rows in a strong year, and the Reserve Pinot Noir of 2000 won the Pinot Noir trophy at the International Wine Challenge in London in 2001. The Reserve carries three moments of the house's early history: the region's first commercial vintage, the cave and a London trophy.

wine.name: Mt Difficulty Bannockburn Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir only, several clones of it blended across the house's Bannockburn vineyards.
wine.sites: Estate vineyards and vineyards the winery manages on the south side of the Kawarau at Bannockburn, the earlier plantings above all, on soils that run from open gravels to heavier clays.
wine.making: Part of the fruit goes into the ferments as whole bunches, from about a tenth to a fifth or more by vintage. The wine then rests ten to twelve months in barrel on its full lees, about a fifth of the barrels new in vintages such as 2021 and 2022, with the malolactic fermentation in the spring; it is racked in late autumn and filtered, but not fined, before bottling.
wine.glass: Red and black cherry, raspberry and blood plum over blueberry and orange peel; fuller and darker than the cooler sub-regions give, with a silky texture, firm, fine grained tannin and bold acidity.
wine.ageing: Open it on release, or give a strong vintage some seven years and more to deepen.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: In 1998 a group of Bannockburn growers began making wine under one label, and Mt Difficulty Bannockburn Pinot Noir blends the house's vineyards on gravel and clay south of the Kawarau. Bannockburn's warmth shows in its cherry and blood plum and its silky, firm tannin.
records.story: Bannockburn's terraces on the south side of the Kawarau were worked for gold in the nineteenth century, and its vineyards came to share the slopes with the old sluicings. In the 1990s the owners of a handful of newly planted vineyards there, who came to be known as the Gang of Four, chose to make wine together under one label rather than each alone. Mt Difficulty's first vintage was 1998. The growers' handshake held until 2004, when the company Mt Difficulty Wines was formed and most of the founding vineyards passed into it. The house went on to bottle some of its vineyards apart: Pipeclay Terrace, from vines planted in 1996 on coarse soils and heavy clay, is released only in strong vintages, and Mansons Farm is made in small quantities. A second label, Roaring Meg, came to stand beside the first. In 2022 Bannockburn became a registered Geographical Indication of its own, within Central Otago. In one bottle the house maps the sub-region: fruit from several vineyards on gravel and clay, blended to show the place rather than one site.

report: The house is not in the library: founded is 1998, the first vintage, in the Otago Daily Times and a Glengarry Wines newsletter (WL114); the growers' handshake became the company Mt Difficulty Wines in 2004 by Supermarket News and a second Otago Daily Times piece.

Living people kept out, none yet in people.json: the founding grower and his wife, who planted several of Bannockburn's first vineyards, their son the long serving winemaker and the winemaker of Gibbston Valley who made the first vintages; pages with their names in the address (The Central App, Rural News) were read but not cited.

The making, sites and clones rest on the house's own fact sheets of 2016, 2018 and 2021 (the 2021 sheet's co-fermented clonal lots, one vintage only, are left out); no sheet read gave the oak's origin or its share of new barrels, so the record says barrel alone.

The glass draws on the house's note of the 2024 and 2022 quoted by Vino Fino (red and black cherry, blueberry, blackberry, satsuma plum, silky fine tannin), Decanter's review of the 2017 (ripe plummy fruit) and New Zealand Winegrowers' line that Bannockburn gives fuller, more tannic Pinot Noir; the ageing on a critic's window of 2030 and more for the 2023.

Roaring Meg as the second label is in Supermarket News, a Woolworths listing and the house's own page (mtdifficulty.nz/wine), which dates its launch to 2004; its naming for a stream of the Kawarau Gorge is in that search's summary and a British merchant's page (Specialist Cellars or Ellis Wines), with the legend of a woman of an 1860s digging party carried over the rapid, one source only and left out.

Left out for want of a second source: a gold medal for the 1998 Pinot Noir at the Air New Zealand Wine Awards of 1999, the winery of 2001, the cellar door of 2003, the barrel hall of 2012, the growers' earlier sales of grapes to Gibbston Valley and Chard Farm, and a sale of the company in 2018 to an American buyer.

New Zealand Winegrowers' winery page says the winery was designed for low energy use with its barrel hall sunk below ground; left out of the story, since the five sources the cap allows went to the dates and the making.
No swap proposed: the Bannockburn Pinot Noir is the house's main Pinot Noir; its single vineyard wines come only in some vintages.

changed: founded: The venture began with a handshake dated 1992 in one account, made its first vintage in 1998 and became a company in 2004 (2003 in one): no founding year is sure, and an empty field is a true answer.

wine.name: Quartz Reef Bendigo Estate Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: All Pinot Noir, grown on the house's own estate at Bendigo.
wine.sites: The Bendigo Estate vineyard, first planted in 1998 on a north facing slope above the east bank of Lake Dunstan, on arid clay, fine gravel and quartz over the reef that names the house; certified biodynamic by Demeter since 2011.
wine.making: Hand picked and destemmed, the fruit is cold soaked for some days, fermented with indigenous yeasts and left on its skins after fermentation, about three weeks in all in vintages such as 2014 and 2021. It then spends twelve to fourteen months in French oak barriques, from about a sixth to a half of them new by vintage, and the 2017 went to bottle unfined and unfiltered.
wine.glass: Black cherry and ripe plum over violet and a hint of cedar, deep in colour and very savoury; weighty and dense, as the warm Bendigo slope makes it, with fine tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and youthful at first, it opens a few years after the vintage and keeps for a decade in a strong year.
wine.serve: A wide Burgundy glass, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius, and an hour's decanting for a young bottle.

label.means: The house's own vineyard at Bendigo Station, first planted in 1998.
The sub-region on the east bank of Lake Dunstan, by New Zealand Winegrowers' account perhaps the warmest in Central Otago.
A registered Geographical Indication lying at about 45 degrees south, inland in the South Island.

records.table: Quartz Reef is named for the reef beneath its warm, north facing slope at Bendigo, first planted in 1998 and farmed biodynamically, where its Bendigo Estate Pinot Noir grows. The house is known as well for its sparkling wine; this is black cherry, plum and violet, dense yet savoury.
records.story: By the house's account, an Austrian born winemaker first looked at the slopes of Bendigo, on the east bank of Lake Dunstan, in 1990, and in 1996 founded Quartz Reef with partners, among them the farmer of Bendigo Station. The house took its name from the quartz reef that runs beneath the vineyard, by its own account the largest quartz deposit in New Zealand. The first vines went into Bendigo Station in 1998, and the first harvest came in 2001. Beside its Pinot Noir the house made sparkling wine by the traditional method, with a second fermentation in bottle, and became known for both. In 2007 it began to convert the vineyard to biodynamic farming, and in 2011 it gained Demeter certification, with its winery certified organic by BioGro. The house also bottles one chosen parcel ferment of a vintage on its own, as its Single Ferment Pinot Noir, beside the Bendigo Estate Pinot Noir. For a sommelier it marks the warm end of Central Otago: dark, dense Pinot Noir from a slope that faces the sun.

cards.front: What lies beneath the vineyard at Bendigo Station, and what did it give the house that farms it?
cards.back: A quartz reef, New Zealand's largest quartz deposit by the house's account; it gave Quartz Reef its name.

cards.back: Conversion began in 2007, and Demeter certification followed in 2011.

questions.exp: The first vines went in in 1998 and gave a first harvest in 2001; 1996 is the founding and 2007 the start of the biodynamic conversion.

report: The house is not in the library: founded is 1996, as the house's story page and the secondary pages read (Glengarry Wines, Vind, Fine Wine Delivery) give it and as the region line has it; the house's home page says 1998, the year of planting, and the house's timeline puts the start of the biodynamic conversion in 2001 where its other pages and the secondaries say 2007.

Living people kept out, none yet in people.json: the Austrian born founding winemaker and his two partners, a Cromwell businessman and the farmer of Bendigo Station; the critic whose review the house reprints is not named, and New Zealand Winegrowers' page on the founder is not cited because its address names him.

The making gathers the house's own pages by vintage: hand picked, a cold soak, indigenous yeasts with a small share of whole bunches, twenty four days on skins and fourteen months with twenty four per cent new barriques in 2014, half new and unfined and unfiltered in 2017; the 2004 was fined with egg white, so no habit of never fining is claimed.

The glass draws on the reviews the house reprints of the 2017 (deep, fragrant, weighty, very savoury, ripe cherry and plum) and the 2018 (black cherry, dark berry, violet, fine tannin), and on the library's dense Bendigo Pinot Noir; the ageing on Decanter's windows of about three to ten years from the vintage.
One secondary page calls the reef gold bearing; with no second source the record does not say so.

Left out for want of a second source: that sparkling wine was the founder's fallback while Pinot Noir was unproven, and that it makes up about three quarters of what the house bottles; the library's region line calls the house's sparkling the region's leading, a judgement this record does not repeat.

The plan's wine name is kept, though the house labels its Pinot Noirs variously as Bendigo Estate, Bendigo Estate Single Vineyard and Bendigo; the house's product page for a Single Ferment of 2020 carries the title Bendigo Estate Pinot Noir, so the refuter should confirm which bottling each review describes; the record keeps the 2014 and 2017 Bendigo Estate pages for its making.
No swap proposed.

changed: wine.making: A profile of 2013 has the fruit destemmed, so the small share of whole bunches is cut; a cold soak, indigenous yeasts, a maceration after fermentation and twelve to fourteen months in barriques, fifteen to fifty per cent new by vintage, are in four accounts.

wine.label[1].means: New Zealand Winegrowers calls Bendigo the warmest sub-region on one page and possibly the warmest in its textbook, so the line hedges; the Dunstan Mountains were in no source read.

story: The founding partners are the owner of Bendigo Station and others, no Cromwell businessman in any source read; the founder first looked at Bendigo in 1990; the Single Ferment is one chosen parcel ferment of a vintage.
others[1].note: Vino Fino's note: each parcel is fermented apart and the one ferment of the vintage the house judges the most expressive is bottled on its own.
open: The house's own timeline puts the start of the biodynamic conversion in 2001 against 2007 elsewhere; the record keeps 2007, which two independent accounts give.
The Otago Daily Times and a property listing of the Bendigo estate report a sale of the winery; the record says nothing of owners, so nothing volatile stands.
